CLINICAL COMMUNICATION
Diplopia management in a patient with stiff person syndrome
Denise Skiadopoulos
Illinois Eye Institute, Illinois College of Optometry, Chicago, IL, USA
ARTICLE HISTORY Received 29 September 2022; Revised 8 November 2022; Accepted 24 February 2023 
KEYWORDS Diplopia; prism; stiff man syndrome; stiff person syndrome; strabismus
Introduction
Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is a rare autoimmune disorder that 
is estimated to affect fewer than one million people globally. It 
is progressive and causes muscle rigidity, stiffness, and spasm. 
The most widely accepted cause is autoimmune, with the 
majority of patients exhibiting antibodies against glutamic 
acid decarboxylase (GAD).
1–7 
Reported ocular findings of SPS 
include strabismus, nystagmus, and saccadic dysfunction as 
well as other oculomotor disorders.
1–3 
The following case illus -
trates a patient with SPS-induced strabismus and the role of 
the optometrist in managing the resultant diplopia.
Case report
Visit 1
A 43-year-old African American male presented to an urban 
Urgent Eye Care clinic with a complaint of sudden onset 
vertical diplopia. Systemic history was unremarkable for thyr -
oid conditions, rapid weight loss or weight gain, or change in 
energy level. The patient denied experiencing ptosis, dysgeu -
sia, difficulty breathing, or generalised fatigue.
Visual acuity was 6/6 in each eye; pupils were equal, round, 
and reactive to light; monocular ductions were full; and con -
frontation visual fields were full in each eye. Prism alternating 
cover test revealed a constant left hypertropia that worsened 
in left gaze and on right head tilt. Park’s 3 step was performed 
and the deviation was determined to be a left inferior rectus 
under-action. Slit-lamp examination and intraocular pressure 
measurements were within normal limits. Although 
exophthalmometry revealed 26 mm in the right eye and 24  
mm in the left eye, the dilated fundus examination of both 
eyes was unremarkable, with no choroidal folds present. 
Cranial nerves I through XII were found to be intact and 
symmetric. The patient was sent to the emergency room to 
rule out neurologic or vascular aetiology.
The following day the patient was contacted and reported 
that he was admitted to the emergency room. Thyroid eye 
disease and systemic thyroid conditions were excluded based 
on magnetic resonance imaging and blood analysis. 
Magnetic resonance imaging and computerised tomography 
were used to rule out a compressive lesion or ischaemic 
event. The patient was unsure if myasthenia gravis or sagging 
eye syndrome were specifically investigated on laboratory 
testing or imaging, and further details regarding his testing 
in the emergency room were inaccessible. He was then 
scheduled for a diplopia evaluation in the Pediatric & 
Binocular Vision clinic of an urban eye care centre.
Visit 2 – binocular vision evaluation, 1 month later
Case history revealed that one week after the onset of diplo -
pia, the patient began to have muscle stiffness and difficulty 
walking. He had then been diagnosed with SPS by 
a neurologist. He was managing his diplopia with an eye 
patch and was working with his neurologist to manage his 
mobility difficulties. The patient was unable to perform his 
work as a college career counsellor and was temporarily 
placed on medical leave.
Visual acuity, pupils, extraocular motility, confrontation 
visual fields, and slit lamp remained unremarkable. The ver -

tical strabismus persisted and a constant right exotropia was 
now present at all distances. Distance cover test through the 
current myopic and presbyopic corrections of the patient 
revealed an 8Δ constant right hypotropia and 18Δ constant 
right exotropia. Near cover test through correction revealed 
a 10Δ constant right hypotropia and 12Δ constant right exo -
tropia. The patient did not exhibit any symptoms or signs of 
a saccadic or pursuit dysfunction upon testing, though mono -
cular fixation was unsteady during prism alternating cover 
test. He could not appreciate gross forms.
A prism evaluation was performed in which various 
amounts of horizontal and vertical prism were demonstrated 
under binocular viewing conditions. The patient reported 
relief of diplopia at distance and near with 8Δ base-in and 
10Δ base-up over the right eye. Bifocals with 4Δ base-in in 
each eye, 5 prism dioptres base-up in the right eye, and 5Δ 
base-down in the left eye were prescribed. A follow-up visit 
was scheduled for one month later.
Visit 3–1 month later
The patient presented for follow-up reporting improvements 
in mobility after his neurologist initiated intravenous immu -
noglobulin treatment. Diplopia was largely relieved through 
the prismatic spectacles, but occasional vertical diplopia per -
sisted. He reported experiencing the least amount of diplopia 
immediately after intravenous immunoglobulin treatments.
Distance cover test through the prismatic correction 
revealed 6Δ constant right hypotropia and 6Δ intermittent 
right exotropia; near cover test revealed 2Δ exophoria with 
no vertical deviation. When an additional 1Δ base-up was 
demonstrated over the right eye, the patient reported sub -
jective improvement. The patient now had positive gross 
forms upon stereopsis testing through the prism. A Fresnel 
prism with 1Δ base-up was adhered to the right lens of the 
patient.

Visit 4–1 month later
The patient reported full resolution of diplopia while wearing 
prismatic glasses with Fresnel prisms. The additional 1Δ base- 
up was not ground into a new pair of spectacles due to the 
possibility that the ocular deviation would change through -
out the course of the disease and treatment. He was made 
aware that Fresnel prisms may be adjusted if ocular align -
ment improves or changes as intravenous immunoglobulin 
treatments continue.
Discussion
SPS, also referred to as stiff-man syndrome, is a rare disorder 
with neurologic causes that can result in ocular 
manifestations.
1–3 
Systemically, SPS is characterised by mus -
cle spasms and rigidity
1–6 
as well as lumbar hyperlordosis and 
difficult ambulation.
4 
It has a predilection for females
5 
and 
case reports describe clinical onset ranging from 1 to 76 years 
of age.
1–7 
Though epidemiological data on SPS is limited due 
to its rarity, the currently reported median age of symptom 
onset is 40 years.
4 , 5
While the understood cause is an autoimmune response to 
GAD,
1–7 
a small minority of SPS patients present without anti- 
GAD antibodies.
4–6 
SPS often presents with coexisting auto -
immune conditions (such as type 1 diabetes mellitus and 
thyroid disease) and, less frequently, coexisting cancer (such 
as various carcinomas or non-Hodgkin lymphoma).
5–7
Symptomatic treatment of SPS includes benzodiazepines 
(most commonly diazepam) and baclofen.
1 , 4–7 
Immunotherapy, namely intravenous immunoglobulin and 
azathioprine, has also been used with success,
3–7 
as was 
demonstrated in the patient in this case.
Several ocular findings have been reported in patients 
with SPS ( Table 1 ). GAD is the synthetic enzyme for GABA 
and GABAergic neurons are important in brainstem eye 
movement control.
2 
Since SPS is largely caused by anti-GAD 
antibodies, it follows logically that SPS can affect eye move -
ments. The patient in this case experienced only strabismus, 
but nystagmus and saccadic dysfunction are the most com -
mon ocular findings.
1 
Other findings can include smooth 
pursuit deficits and supranuclear gaze palsy.
1–3
SPS can be deeply debilitating, with one study reporting 
that 17 out of 31 employed SPS patients had to stop working 
as a result of their condition.
5 
While neurologists manage the 
systemic effects of SPS, eye care providers should be aware of 
this rare condition and should remain knowledgeable about 
ocular management. In this case, use of prism in spectacles 
allowed the patient to view his computer and gradually 
return to work despite his difficulties with ambulation. The 
patient reported feeling relieved that he no longer required 
an eye patch for single vision.
This case also illustrates the importance of using Fresnel 
prism in conditions where ocular motility may be variable. 
Because SPS is progressive and the patient is undergoing 
treatment, the ocular deviation may be variable at future 
visits. Fresnel lenses serve as a crucial tool in maintaining 
clear, comfortable binocular vision for the patient.
